posts.title: The autumn course begins: matsutake, saury and the first new rice
posts.excerpt: From this week the counter turns to autumn: pine mushrooms in the clear soup, saury over charcoal and the year's first rice from the clay pot.
posts.content:
Every year there is one morning when the market tells us the season has turned. This year it was the last Tuesday of September: the first basket of matsutake from the hills to the south, and a crate of saury so fat the fishmonger laughed when he lifted the lid.

So from this week the Tsuki course is an autumn course. Here is what to expect, in the order it arrives.

Pine, smoke and steam

  • The clear soup carries matsutake and sea bream in the first dashi of the evening
  • The grill is given to Pacific saury, salted an hour ahead and served with sudachi
  • The rice is the new crop from our field, cooked in the clay pot for your seating

The matsutake season is short and the price moves daily. We keep the course price fixed and simply use more or less of it; please do not be surprised if a slice is thinner one week and thicker the next.

Seats for November open at noon on 1 October. Season-letter readers already have the link.

posts.title: Why we only have nine seats
posts.excerpt: People ask whether we will ever open a second counter, or add tables. The honest answer is in the length of one hinoki plank.
posts.content:
Twice a week someone asks why we do not add a few tables, or open a second room. It would make the book easier, and the bill a little smaller. The honest answer is a matter of distance.

From the cutting board, the chef can reach every plate on the counter without taking a step. From the grill, Daichi can see every guest's face. Nine seats is as far as that reach goes on a nine-metre plank.

A counter is a promise. You see everything we do, and we see that you are happy.

Ren Akagi

What nine seats make possible

Every guest starts together, so every course arrives at the moment it is ready, not when a waiter can carry it. The soup is seasoned to the room's temperature. The rice is lifted when the last guest has finished the grill.

It also means we can talk. Ask about any dish and you will hear where it came from, usually from the person who cooked it. For many guests, that conversation is the part they remember.

posts.title: A beginner's guide to sake pairing at the counter
posts.excerpt: Five glasses, three temperatures, one simple idea: what Sayo is thinking about when she pours, and how to ask for what you like.
posts.content:
If you have only ever drunk sake cold, or only hot, the pairing is a good place to start. Sayo pours five glasses across the evening, and each one is chosen for the course it meets, not for its label.

Three temperatures

  • Chilled, around ten degrees, for the first bites and the raw fish: crisp, bright and a little floral
  • Cool, as it comes from the cellar, for the simmered dishes: round and savoury
  • Warm, around forty-five degrees, for the grill and the rice: wide, soft and long

Warming sake is not a way of hiding a cheap bottle. Some of the best sake on our list opens up only when it is warm, the way a red wine opens in a decanter.

How to ask

You do not need any words beyond drier, softer or more like that one. Sayo will change the next glass. And the tea and soda pairing is made with the same care, for anyone not drinking tonight.

posts.title: Cooking over white charcoal
posts.excerpt: Hard oak charcoal burns hot, clean and almost without smoke. Daichi on why he lights it at four, and how he reads it by colour.
posts.content:
The grill behind seats one to three is fed with white charcoal: oak, fired slowly for days and then smothered in ash and earth until it rings like metal when two pieces touch.

It takes nearly an hour to come up to heat, which is why Daichi lights it at four o'clock, long before the first guest arrives. Once it is going, it burns hot and steady for the whole evening, with very little smoke.

Reading the fire

There is no thermometer. Daichi reads the charcoal by its colour and by the sound of fat landing on it. Orange with a grey skin is for fish skin; a deep red glow is for wagyu; the cooler edges of the grill are where the rice crackers are toasted.

Gas cooks the food. Charcoal also perfumes it. The fish should taste of the fire for one second, not one minute.

Daichi Mori

If you sit at the grill end, you may be asked to help with the fan. Most guests accept.

posts.title: The owan: why the soup is the quiet centre of the course
posts.excerpt: Kelp and bonito, drawn at six in the evening, and a lid you lift slowly. The third course is the one the kitchen worries about most.
posts.content:
In a kappo course the clear soup arrives third, after the opening bites and before the knife. It is the most modest-looking dish of the evening and the one the kitchen worries about most.

The dashi is drawn fresh for each seating: kelp soaked from the morning, brought nearly to a simmer, then a handful of shaved bonito that is strained off after barely a minute. It is seasoned with salt and a few drops of light soy, tasted, and tasted again.

Lift the lid slowly

We serve it in black lacquer with a red interior and a fitted lid, so the aroma waits for you. Lift the lid towards you, smell first, then drink straight from the bowl. Chopsticks are for the matsutake and the fish.

posts.title: Rice last: the clay pot at the end of every course
posts.excerpt: Every course ends with rice from a clay pot, cooked for your seating and opened at the counter. Second bowls are expected.
posts.content:
The last savoury course is always rice. Not a token spoonful: a full clay pot cooked for your seating, opened at the counter in a cloud of steam, with pickles and a bowl of red miso soup.

Our rice comes from one family field below the mountains, milled every two weeks so it never sits long as white rice. In October the new crop arrives, and for a month the rice course is simply that: new rice, nothing added, the clearest taste of the year.

The crust at the bottom

If you are lucky, Ren will scrape the golden crust from the bottom of the pot and pass it along the counter. Some guests book the second seating for this reason alone.

Anything left in the pot is shaped into rice balls and wrapped for you to take home.

posts.title: Winter crab, and our new-year closing
posts.excerpt: Snow crab joins the course from November to February, and the counter closes for the first week of January while the lanterns are re-papered.
posts.content:
Snow crab season opens in early November, and from then until the end of February the crab appears on the Beni course and as a supplement on the others. The price follows the market; we tell you the evening's price when you sit down.

Closed 1 — 7 January

Every new year we close for a week. The kitchen is scrubbed, the hinoki counter is sanded, the knives go to the sharpener and the two lanterns over the door are re-papered by hand. We reopen on the eighth with a small new-year course.

Thank you for another year at the counter. We look forward to seeing you, a little brighter, in the new one.
